Introducing 'The Second Order', a new monthly newsletter on the systems, shifts, and forces redefining workplace learning. The first of those shifts is already underway, and none of it registers as a problem. The learning function is still doing exactly the job it was built for, and that job was defined when producing learning was slow, expensive and dependent on scarce expertise. AI has removed all three of those constraints, leaving a function that can hit every one of its KPIs and still be aimed at a target the business has moved past. The Second Order follows shifts like that one from the point they begin to the point they force a decision. Subscribe to our newsletter for more insights.

Daqstra is the AI-native operating layer for complex hardware teams, helping engineers connect every instrument, understand every test, and safely run what comes next. Great hardware is built through cycles of testing, failure, and discovery, and testing infrastructure shouldn’t bottleneck that engineering. Yet teams across aerospace, energy, and robotics assemble test setups from NI systems, PLCs, vendor software, custom electronics, and in-house code that were never designed to work together. Engineers end up rebuilding integrations, searching across machines, and reconstructing what happened before they can learn from a test. Founders Anchit Kumar and Darell Chua built Daqstra after experiencing this firsthand while firing liquid rocket engines in the Mojave. Daqstra records commands, telemetry, configurations, and engineering context in one system, giving its AI the context to compare runs, trace anomalies back to source data, and help prepare repeatable test sequences through a controlled API. Instead of stopping at a summary, Daqstra closes the loop from observation to the next test while engineers remain in control. Daqstra is now used day-to-day in active aerospace programs and has signed an industrial energy pilot targeting $100K+ in annual savings. If you lead test, integration, propulsion, or validation at a complex hardware company, Daqstra wants to hear from you. Congrats on the launch, Anchit and Darell! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gdSrABY7

Last week, I completed the Spring Fellowship with AI Alignment at UC San Diego . Special thanks to Aldan Creo and Kevin Zhang for organizing this! It was a valuable experience to discuss, question, and think through one of the most pressing problems in technology today: how do we build AI systems that are not just powerful, but reliable, interpretable, and aligned with human intent? AI is probably gonna become one of the most influential technologies of our lifetimes. But despite how useful these systems already are, we still do not fully understand how they represent our world internally, why they make certain decisions, or how they will behave when given more autonomy across real products and institutions. This matters because the hard part is not only making models smarter - its making sure they do what we actually mean. As a naive example, if a CEO asks an advanced GPT 10 that is integrated everywhere to cut compute costs, what if it just nukes the database? (has happened btw) Even more pressing - what if a random website the AI consults is prompt-injected to do some harmful stuff? We don't have a real solution to that either. In a real company, hospital, financial system, or government workflow, this becomes a serious product and engineering problem. That is why alignment cannot just be treated as abstract philosophy. It is also about better engineering: guardrails, evaluations, interpretability, observability, accountability, human oversight, and careful product design. Frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made impressive progress here, but then as AI gets integrated into nearly every tool used by individuals, companies, and governments, I think alignment will become one of the bigger bottlenecks to realizing the upside of this technology. The fellowship helped me see AI alignment less as a distant theoretical concern and more as a practical question worth thinking about: How do we build systems and products that are capable enough to be useful, but constrained and understandable enough to be trusted? #AI #UCSanDiego

A few days ago, Arnav Lohiya , Tejas Shah , and I were on the Amazon Kiro YouTube channel walking through AllVoice, the voice-controlled Chrome extension we built in 24 hours for blind and low-vision users at the ASU Kiro Spark Challenge. Brian asked what advice we'd give students heading into an industry moving this fast. My take: AI shouldn't replace the learning itself. Use it as a tool, learn from it, but don't get dependent on it. Learn the fundamentals deeply first, because that's what lets you actually direct AI well instead of just accepting whatever it gives you. Then use it to build things you couldn't have built otherwise. The part I keep coming back to is the ethics gate. Pure synchronous function, four rules, and if it blocks a command, the executor is just gone. There's no code path to it. We built it that way because the thing deciding whether a blind user's password field gets touched can't be something that fails quietly on a weird edge case. Someone in the live chat called out, "Adding ethical rules as steering files is a smart idea." That genuinely made my day. What made the three-person team actually work: we wrote the shared data contract before anyone touched code. I had the pipeline, Tejas had the ethics gate, and Arnav had the UI. When we brought it together, it fit. That's the spec. Thanks to Brian Beach , Helen Hasbun , and the Kiro and Amazon Web Services (AWS) team for having us. And Arnav and Tejas, good team. Full hour on the Kiro channel if you want to watch: https://lnkd.in/gtziJSMt #KiroSparkChallenge #AgenticAI #Accessibility #AWS #BuildInPublic ...more ...more

Out of 50 teams at Arizona State University, our team (Aman, Tejas, and Arnav) built AllVoice, a voice-controlled Chrome Extension copilot for blind and low-vision users. We chose the Ethics frame and built a six-stage pipeline with a mandatory Ethics Logic Gate, a pure function that blocks privacy violations before they reach the page. Passwords, payment fields, and PII, if it's unsafe, the action never executes. We also got nominated for the Build signal, which meant a lot because we went deep on Kiro's toolkit: a three-layer spec (requirements, design, tasks), five steering files, eight agent hooks automating everything from type checks to ethics gate integrity reviews, and MCP for live web access. 103 tests. We used Kiro hooks to generate posts at key milestones, showing the community what spec-driven, ethical AI development looks like in practice. The judges valued that transparency. This was my first hackathon ever. Walking in, I didn't know what to expect. Walking out with Best in Story, a Build nomination, and Grand Prize runners-up, that's something I'll carry for a long time. This experience reinforced something I deeply believe: accessibility, AI, and ethics aren't trade-offs. They're layers of the same system. AllVoice proves that software can be powerful and principled at the same time. This event pushed me to think about AI agents beyond just prompting. I attended Camp AI Seattle, hosted by Auth0 , and spent the evening seeing demos, hearing from people building in the space, and talking with other engineers and founders about where agentic AI is actually heading. A few things that stood out to me: * Human-in-the-loop still matters. One demo showed an agent that could book a flight and add it directly to a calendar, while still keeping the user involved at important decision points. Okta * Authentication becomes much more important when agents can take actions. I saw how agents can handle internal company workflows like requesting access, resetting passwords, or connecting employees to other tools, but only if permissions and identity are handled correctly. Ravenna * Observability is becoming essential for MCP and agent workflows. Being able to see whether an API or MCP call actually worked in real time becomes incredibly valuable once agents start chaining tools together. APIContext * Agents are moving beyond software. I also learned about using agents for testing physical devices and started thinking more about the safety implications when AI can affect real-world systems. FlintLab Inc. One question I kept coming back to throughout the night was: As AI gets better at generating code, where does prompt engineering end and software engineering begin? Beyond the technical discussions, I also got to meet a lot of people who are genuinely excited about building in this space and came away with some great conversations and new connections. Thanks to Auth0 and everyone involved in Camp AI Seattle for putting together such a great evening. Looking forward to building more in this space. #AI #AIAgents #MCP #SoftwareEngineering #SeattleTech #ArtificialIntelligence

🎙️ One week in San Francisco. First hackathon here. 3rd place + a special prize. I moved to SF 7 days ago and was still finding my footing when I signed up for the a1mobile Voice AI Hackathon at frontiertower -- solo, after my friend's registration didn't get approved. No team, no idea what I was going to build. Right before the event started, a guy walked up with zero introduction and just asked, "Are you looking for a team?" That was Ali Amjad, turned out he already had a team going with Aaquila M. and Piotr Kram, and I joined in. Calling ourselves WinTeam turned out to be fitting. We picked a problem a lot of cafe and restaurant managers deal with constantly: when an employee can't make a shift, the manager has to drop what they're doing, call people one by one, explain the shift details, wait for a yes, text a confirmation, and manually update the schedule. It eats up hours every week. So we built ShiftRescue -- a voice agent that handles the entire process. It calls through the employee roster, talks to them in English, Spanish, or Hindi (and can switch languages mid-conversation), gets a yes or no, sends an SMS confirmation once someone agrees, and updates the manager's dashboard automatically. We used a1mobile for the phone number and Vapi to handle STT, TTS and voice orchestration. We also ran VoiceOS (YC P25) on top of the product, which won us a separate prize. It was great talking to Kasim Inan , Darryl Foong , Maksim Liashch along with the rest of the a1mobile and VoiceOS folks who stuck around to give feedback and talk through ideas. Also got to demo ShiftRescue for Utkarsh Bajpai along the way, a definite highlight. Congratulations to the other winners and all fellow cracked builders who were there! I was told not to picture a pink elephant in sunglasses. I pictured it instantly. Then I "remembered" a word that was never on the screen. Then I completely blew a guess about the height of Everest. By the end of the hour I'd failed multiple psychology experiments in a row - and understood how AI actually "thinks" better than any textbook ever managed. (New here? Every week a group of us picks something from our field - AI, finance, cloud, psychology - and breaks it down for everyone else, then argues about it. This week was Kevin Doshi 's turn.) And instead of slides full of theory, he just ran the experiments on us, live, and watched the whole room fall for every single one. What he was really showing: → "Peanut butter and ___" - your brain autocompletes before you choose to. So does an LLM. → Flash the words Dream, Bed, Night, Pillow… and half of us were sure we'd seen "Sleep." It was never there. Your brain filled it in - the human version of an AI hallucination. → Two answers, same meaning: we trust whichever one sounds more confident. Even when it's wrong. His closing line stuck with me: You didn't see the world. You saw what your brain expected. So next time an AI sounds certain, ask what your own head is doing - showing you reality, or just predicting what comes next? One of the most memorable sessions we've run. Kevin Doshi didn't explain cognitive bias to us - he made us feel it in real time, then held up the mirror to AI. Hard to forget a lesson you personally fell for. publications.title: A Multimodal Approach for Skin Lesion Diagnosis
publications.subtitle: IEEE Xplore
publications.description: Inspection by dermatologists remains the standard for skin cancer diagnosis, but it can be subjective and prone to error. We explore the potential of machine learning for dermoscopic image classification using 10,000 pigmented skin lesions. Although convolutional neural networks are powerful tools for skin lesion classification by themselves, by incorporating patient-specific textual data, we aim to improve the accuracy and accessibility of diagnosis. We propose multiple multimodal models: transfer learning and multimodal transformers. These multimodal approaches aim to utilise both dermoscopic images and corresponding patient-specific data, such as lesion location and patient demographics. Our multimodal model with the best overall evaluation is the multimodal transformer model which combines a vision transformer and a text transformer. It achieved an accuracy of 93.21% and an AUROC of 0.9860.

projects.title: ARRAI
projects.description: ARRAI is an AI-powered inspection system designed to pair directly with wearable devices like Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses to modernize heavy machinery inspections. Instead of carrying clipboards or manually documenting findings, inspectors can simply record components in the field using the glasses, capturing first-person video and images hands-free. That media is automatically ingested into ARRAI’s cloud pipeline, where computer vision and audio analysis models detect component-level defects and anomalies. A fine-tuned language model then converts those structured detections into clear, standardized inspection issues and generates a CAT-style report aligned with industry documentation standards. By combining wearable capture, automated analysis, and structured report generation, ARRAI transforms raw field footage into professional inspection documentation in near real time, reducing manual effort while improving accuracy and consistency.

projects.title: Lexora
projects.description: I built and deployed an end-to-end cloud AI system that transforms raw contract PDFs into structured, clause-level risk insights and negotiation guidance. The platform uses a dual-model architecture that combines deterministic machine learning with grounded LLM reasoning to avoid hallucination-prone, LLM-only workflows. At its core is ClauseRiskNet, a custom clause classification and risk-scoring model (0–100) with confidence estimates, supported by multi-stage inference fallbacks (ONNX → sklearn → heuristic rules) to ensure reliability and reproducibility. The system implements a full document pipeline, including PDF extraction, clause segmentation, ML inference, risk aggregation, and persistent storage for auditability. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) layer powers negotiation playbooks and redline suggestions using clause-scoped TF-IDF retrieval and schema-validated LLM outputs. The production frontend was built with Next.js and TypeScript, featuring synchronized PDF viewing and interactive clause exploration, while the backend runs as a Dockerized FastAPI service with PostgreSQL on cloud infrastructure. The system was designed with a strong emphasis on explainability, determinism, and auditability over black-box summarization.

The code was written yesterday. Why will it take 5+ weeks to go live? For decades in software development, writing code was the known bottleneck. We all knew it. We built complex processes and planning cycles around the fact that one difficult, essential thing would take a long time to complete. We optimized around engineering. But that doesn’t make sense anymore. Coding speed is no longer the constraint. Coordination is. Yet, we are still running modern, high-velocity output through legacy, low-velocity governance. When you spend millions to accelerate engineering only to stall at the approval line, you haven’t actually sped up the organization. You've just built a bigger traffic jam at the gate. The enterprise advantage no longer belongs to who can write code the fastest. It belongs to who can clear its path. Read more from Richard Newcomb , Senior Director, FDE → https://lnkd.in/grAx_WKc

Last weekend, Terac sponsored a track at the Berkeley AI Hackathon built around a simple challenge: Can you collect your own human data and use it to make an AI system better? Congratulations to the winners, MatchVision, who made soccer more accessible for blind and low-vision fans ahead of the 2026 World Cup. They started with a vision-language model and quickly discovered something surprising: modern VLMs are actually pretty bad at understanding what matters in a soccer match. The ball is small. Important actions happen off-ball. Crowd reactions don't explain why something happened. And generic video captioning models often miss the context that makes the game understandable. So instead of accepting the model's output, they built a human feedback pipeline. Using Terac, they collected annotations describing what an announcer should actually say during key moments in a match. They also collected gaze heatmaps showing where humans naturally focus their attention during play. Those two signals became training data. One taught the model where to look. And the other taught the model what was worth saying. The result wasn't just a better soccer accessibility product. It was a great example of a broader trend we're seeing across AI. For years, progress came from bigger models and bigger datasets. Increasingly, the bottleneck is becoming access to high-quality human judgment. The teams that win won't necessarily be the ones with the biggest models. They'll be the ones that can most effectively turn human expertise into training data, evaluations, and feedback loops. Shoutout to the incredible judges from the Terac team Giovanni Borgogno , Nicolás Russo , Moritz Kamke , Germán Fernández , and Vaibhav Vasudevan ! Also, a shoutout to the runners-up, Captain Ddoski, who tackled a completely different but equally important problem: helping AI systems determine whether information is actually trustworthy before acting on it.

projects.title: Quantum Optimization Algorithm To Efficiently Route Public Transportation In Cities
projects.description: Cars are one of the biggest polluters of greenhouse gases and to reduce their impact on the environment, there needs to be a nation-wide shift towards the use of public transportation - specifically the use of buses. Designing new bus routes can help buses arrive more frequently on time, especially during rush hour, which is an incentive for people to use buses. The Urban Transit Routing Problem (UTRP) is an NP-hard optimization problem, solved with heuristic algorithms that output approximate solutions, that focuses on constructing bus routes from an existing road network. The purpose of this project is to use quantum computing to solve the UTRP by minimizing a road network’s average travel time (ATT), a measure of the average travel time for all passengers to travel between all pairs of bus stops. My engineering goal was to use quantum computing, which has a theoretical advantage over heuristics in solving NP-hard problems, to produce routes with a lower ATT than heuristics for Mandl’s Swiss benchmark and existing bus routes in downtown Seattle. My algorithm achieved an ATT of 10.11 minutes for the benchmark, which is an improvement over current UTRP solvers. Additionally, my algorithm decreased the ATT in a section of downtown Seattle by 53%. This research supported my engineering goals by showing the feasibility of using quantum computers to develop routes with a lower ATT than both classical heuristic methods for a benchmark and existing bus routes in downtown Seattle.

It was a great week at the IEEE World Congress on SERVICES 2026 in Sydney earlier this July, and I'm still thinking about the insightful conversations. I had the honour of giving an invited talk at the IEEE Quantum Software 2026 Symposium: "When Quantum Meets AI in the Cloud: A Software Systems Perspective on Resource Orchestration." My argument was simple: Quantum advantage will not arrive through hardware advancement alone. It will also depend on the quantum software systems and cloud services that decide what runs where, when, and at what cost. That layer still feels wide open to me, and it may be where our community can move most quickly. Two of our papers at the congress approach that problem from different ends: - QBugLM (IEEE QSW 2026) starts with the developer, asking whether LLM agents can genuinely debug quantum programs. We give the community an agentic benchmark framework to measure what these agents can actually do in finding and repairing bugs for quantum software. - QCOEM (IEEE CLOUD 2026) starts with the platform, treating quantum cloud orchestration as a multi-objective problem where fidelity, waiting time, and cost rarely agree. Here we solve those trade-offs with evolutionary optimisation, which complements the deep reinforcement learning angle we took earlier in DRLQ and QFOR. Both point toward what we are building at QuantumAI.Cloud (QAC) intersection: quantum as a cloud resource, and AI as the layer that helps developers and orchestrators reason about it. 🎉 Huge thanks to the organisers, my supervisor Muhammad Usman , my co-authors and students Tam Pham and Andrew Pham , who together did the great work. activity.title: Shipping the CRM Agent in Surface today. The interesting part is that it treats CRM maintenance as a continuous decision problem, not a sync. Most CRM automation is plumbing. It moves fields between systems when a trigger fires, but nobody is deciding what should actually change. So the underlying problem never gets solved: records still go stale, contacts stay half-filled, deals sit in the wrong stage because a human never got to them. You've automated the moving of data, not the judgment about it. This matters because everything downstream inherits the quality of the CRM underneath it. Routing, scoring, forecasting, reporting all read from that data. When reps fall behind on upkeep, and they always do, the decay propagates into every system that depends on it. We built an agent that does the deciding. It runs as a reconciliation loop, not an event handler. It reads the current state, compares it against what the underlying activity implies should be true, and only acts on the gaps it can justify. A call happened but wasn't logged, so log it. A contact is missing a firmographic we already have, so fill it. A deal has had no activity in 40 days but sits in a stage that implies momentum, so flag or move it. The hard part was doing this safely against a live CRM a whole team depends on. Every action is written with provenance, so it corrects records without overwriting what a human deliberately set, and you can always see what changed and why. An agent that silently rewrites your CRM is worse than the problem it solves. It plugs into HubSpot and Salesforce. The effect is that your CRM's data quality stops being a function of how disciplined your reps were this week. ...more

Shipping ad analytics in Surface today. The technically interesting part is what makes it different from bolting on another reporting layer. The core problem with ad attribution isn't tooling, it's incentive structure. Ad platforms report on their own performance. They're graded on volume, optimized to show you signals that justify continued spend, and architecturally isolated from what actually happens to a lead after the click. You can run a campaign for months that looks healthy by platform metrics while the leads it generates are low intent, wrong ICP, or churning early. The platform never sees that signal. It keeps optimizing toward more of the same. The fix isn't another dashboard. It's closing the loop at the data layer. Because Surface runs lead capture, enrichment, and content performance on a single system, we can tie every ad dollar back to actual lead quality as it's being scored. Not after a quarterly attribution audit. When a lead converts, decays, or disqualifies, that signal propagates back to the spend data immediately. The data isn't crossing a gap between disconnected systems, it lives in one place. We also added industry and ICP benchmarking using anonymized peer data. Knowing your cost per lead in a vacuum tells you almost nothing. Knowing whether that number is out of range for companies selling to the same buyer is a different question. The hard part was making benchmarks useful without being misleading. Bucketing by ICP and industry required enough signal density per segment to be meaningful, and we're careful about where we have that and where we don't. What this unlocks is earlier course correction. You can know whether an ad is working 70-80% faster than waiting for downstream revenue data to confirm what the platform already obscured. That compression matters most in the first weeks of a new campaign, when the decisions about scaling or killing spend are still reversible. ...more

The pages bringing us the most traffic had nothing in common with what we were publishing. Here's what we changed: We were doing proper keyword research with search volume, difficulty scores, and competitor gap analysis, so every topic we picked had a real reason behind it. Then I sorted every page on our site by traffic, and a handful of them were doing almost all the work. Nothing we had published in months looked anything like them. We had been trying to guess which topics would work while sitting on a list of the ones that already had. A keyword tool tells you what a lot of people search for. Your own traffic tells you which of those searches actually ended up on your site. So we stopped starting from keywords and started starting from what had already worked: 1/ Pull your top pages by traffic out of Google Analytics. 2/ Compile them into one document, so the pattern across them is visible in one place. 3/ Run that through a Claude SEO skill that pulls the AEO and SEO keywords those pages already rank for. 4/ Write more in that same shape, aimed at the same buyer questions. 5/ Review every draft before it ships, because AI writing that nobody edited is how you end up with slop on your own domain. 6/ Publish, then check analytics again and build on whatever moved. The review step is the one people skip and it is the one that decides whether this compounds or wrecks your site. A model can match a structure, but it cannot tell you when a paragraph says nothing. All of it runs inside Surface, from the analytics pull through to publish. Most content plans get built from what the market searches for. Very few get built from what your own site has already proven.

I built a Slack bot that debugs our production issues before any engineer even notices them. It sits on our alerts channel. The moment a monitor fires, a Claude agent picks up the alert, queries Axiom and a read-only copy of our Postgres, and posts a root-cause writeup right back in the thread. You can reply to steer the investigation, ask it for the list of impacted records, whatever you need. I fired a test alert at it just to see if the plumbing worked. Instead of parsing the alert and stopping there, it pivoted to the database on its own and surfaced a real, ongoing bug that nobody had reported. It laid out the mechanism and the blast radius over the last day, and flagged that the same thing had happened once before, months earlier, then gone quiet. Hours later a teammate hit the exact same bug by hand while testing something unrelated. By then the bot had already scoped it: the affected records, the root cause, and the fix. An agent can rip through log and database queries faster than any engineer. It pulled a full day of data and the exact impacted records in the time it takes to read the alert. But judgment is still the bottleneck: knowing which query to run, whether a number is actually a problem, what to do about it. The bot is fast hands. Someone still has to decide.

My teammates, Aryan Achuthan , Aryan Jain , Kabilesh Yuvaraj , and I, built Open Tix. The project started from an idea we pitched, a ticketing platform designed to address the ticket scalping problem. Today, once a ticket is sold, organizers lose control over how it’s resold. With OpenTix, tickets are minted as NFTs on the XRP Ledger, which makes each ticket verifiable on-chain and allows organizers to set resale price caps and receive royalties on secondary sales. The goal was to show how programmable tickets could reduce fraud, limit extreme markups, and give organizers more control over their ticket markets. At events, tickets can be scanned with a QR code that verifies ownership directly on-chain. In 9 hours, we built a working full stack prototype using React + Vite, Node.js/Express, and MongoDB, integrating XRPL NFTs (XLS-20) with xrpl.js to mint tickets, handle purchases, and verify ownership. It's been a while... 😊 And a lot has changed... . . . I've never been a fan of LinkedIn accomplishment posts. publications.title: Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring for Algorithm Tracing and Problem-Solving in AI Education
publications.subtitle: ACL 2026 21st Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications
publications.description: Students learning algorithms often need support as they interpret traces, debug reasoning errors, and apply procedures across unfamiliar problem instances. In this paper, we present KITE (Knowledge-Informed Tutoring Engine), a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based intelligent tutoring system designed to serve as a classroom teaching assistant for algorithmic reasoning and problem-solving tasks. KITE uses an intent-aware Socratic response strategy to tailor support to different student needs, responding with targeted hints, guiding questions, and progressive scaffolding intended to strengthen students' algorithmic problem-solving ability. To keep responses aligned with course content, KITE uses a multimodal RAG pipeline that retrieves relevant information from course materials. We evaluate KITE using three forms of assessment: RAGAs-based metrics for response grounding and quality, expert evaluation of pedagogical quality, and a simulated student pipeline in which a weaker language model interacts with KITE across two-turn dialogues and produces revised answers after receiving feedback. Results indicate that KITE produces contextually grounded and pedagogically appropriate responses. Further, using simulated students, KITE's feedback helped the student models produce more accurate follow-up responses on procedural and tracing questions, suggesting that its scaffolding can support algorithmic problem-solving. This work contributes a tutoring architecture and an evaluation approach for assessing retrieval-grounded explanations and scaffolded problem-solving feedback.

publications.title: Pattern-based knowledge component extraction from student code using representation learning
publications.subtitle: Educational Data Mining 2026
publications.description: Personalized instruction aims to provide learners with support that adapts to their individual knowledge and progress toward learning objectives. Discovering and tracing Knowledge Components (KCs) is an important step in building accurate models of student learning. However, KC discovery in computer science education is challenging due to the open-ended nature of programming, wide variability in student solutions, and intertwined use of programming structures in code. We address these challenges with a pattern-based KC discovery method that uses a data-driven approach to define KCs as recurring structural patterns in student code that reveal persistent patterns of struggle and mastery in students' solutions. We then evaluate the discovered KCs using expert evaluation and statistical student modeling to demonstrate their effectiveness in capturing student learning and struggles. We propose a framework for modeling students' learning by deriving pattern-based KCs from student code through a three-stage process. First, an attention-based code representation model identifies Abstract Syntax Tree subtrees most relevant to code correctness. Second, a Variational Autoencoder abstracts these subtrees into a smooth latent space, capturing structural similarity across student submissions. Third, the resulting representations are clustered into pattern-based KCs. To assess the effectiveness of pattern-based KCs for modeling students' learning, we adapt the Deep Knowledge Tracing model to incorporate these KCs, demonstrating significant improvements in predictive performance over baseline KT methods. Additionally, the learning curve analysis showed alignment between the derived KCs and learning theory.

publications.subtitle: Intelligent Hospital
publications.description: Stress and depression are two major mental health-related concerns that affect people of varying ages, ranging from teenagers to working class people to senior citizens. As behavioral, physiological, and digital trace data continues to be more accessible, computational models (especially AI-based ones) have become considered a promising solution to stress and mental health assessment. The current paper is a review of the recent research on AI-based stress and depression detection and tries to describe the way the field is developing. The diversity of the works is categorized broadly based on model type, input modality, data source, and evaluation strategy. Classical applications for machine learning remain quite prevalent, particularly for structured data such as EEG signals and questionnaire measurements. DL models and transformer architectures use of transformer-based architectures seems to be effective at physiological signal analysis and text inputs, but reported performance fluctuates. Vision-based models, particularly those using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on static image data such as facial scans or psychological drawings, are widely used. The use of Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal systems remains limited. Performance across reviewed studies was primarily evaluated using Accuracy, F1-score, and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Reported accuracies generally ranged from 74% to 98%, though results vary significantly depending on whether subject-independent validation was used. Some of the limitations in the literature we synthesized are - limited interpretability, inconsistent data standards, virtually no longitudinal modeling, and very little manifestation or clinical validation. This article unites these findings and identifies common gaps and recommends where the field might want to go next - including more standardized datasets, increased interpretability, and practical validation.

publications.title: Automated Program Repair of Uncompilable Student Code
publications.subtitle: Proceedings of the 57th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V.2 (SIGCSE TS 2026)
publications.description: A significant portion of student programming submissions in CS1 learning environments are uncompilable, limiting their use in student modeling and downstream knowledge tracing. Traditional modeling pipelines often exclude these cases, discarding observations of student learning. This study investigates automated program repair as a strategy to recover uncompilable code while preserving students' structural intent for use in student modeling. Within this framework, we assess large language models (LLMs) as repair agents under high- and low-context prompting conditions. Repairs were evaluated for compilability, edit distance, and preservation of students' original structure and logic. While all models produced compilable repairs, they differed in how well they preserve students' control flow and code structure, affecting their pedagogical utility. By recovering uncompilable submissions, this work enables richer and more comprehensive analyses of learners' coding processes and development over time.

publications.title: Transparent communication for residential heating decarbonization: A content analysis of heat pump marketing in Canada
publications.subtitle: Energy Research & Social Science, Elsevier
publications.description: Information transparency helps in building trust between intermediary stakeholders and adopters. Potential adopters seek information as they are learning about a new technology to make an informed decision. To this end, this article analyzes how intermediary installers communicate and market heat pumps, an important technology in residential decarbonization. Marketing communication by heat pump installers has been analyzed using an inductively and deductively developed coding system. Results show that 89 % of the 90 installers did not provide an estimate of the total cost of the equipment that homeowners can expect if they decide to adopt. This highlights areas of information that is missing, known as information gaps, that can be improved to increase heat pump adoption. The results reveal a tendency to over emphasize the energy efficiency improvements and expected utility cost savings from heat pump installation which were discussed by 84 %, and 67 % of the installers respectively. Building on the theories of diffusion of innovation, energy transitions, and corporate social responsibility, these findings reveal critical gaps in information transparency that undermines federal rebate program efforts to increase adoption.

publications.title: Neuropsychological detection and prediction using machine learning algorithms: a comprehensive review
publications.subtitle: Journal of Intelligent Medicine, Elsevier
publications.description: Neuropsychological disorders (e.g., dementia, epilepsy, brain cancer, autism, stroke, and multiple sclerosis) adversely affect the quality of life of patients and their families; moreover, in some instances, they may lead to loss of life. The primary aim was to evaluate and compare the use of machine learning in neuropsychological research in contrast to traditional approaches such as through case studies. This was achieved by referring to earlier studies on this subject. This article presented the use of support vector machines (SVMs) and convolutional neural networks (CNN) for detecting and predicting neuropsychological diseases, such as dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Challenges in using these models include data availability, quality, variability, model interpretability, and validation. Experimental findings have demonstrated the potential of these models in this field. It has been shown that SVM models are robust and efficient in processing and classifying data, particularly in neuroimaging applications, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). CNNs have excelled in handling visual input; thus, they have been used in neuroimaging segregation, recognition, and classification, with applications in brain tumor segmentation, radiation therapy, robotic neurosurgery, and disease prediction. Future research will explore asymmetric differences among left- and right-handed patients, incorporate longitudinal studies, and utilize larger sample sizes. The use of machine learning models has the potential to revolutionize the diagnosis and treatment of neuropsychological diseases, allowing for early detection and intervention. This approach could offer significant advantages to healthcare, such as cost-effective diagnosis and treatment, to help save lives and preserve the quality of life of patients.

publications.title: A systematic study on integrating blockchain in healthcare for electronic health record management and tracking medical supplies
publications.subtitle: Journal of Cleaner Production, Elsevier
publications.description: In the current landscape of swiftly evolving technology, security remains a paramount concern. Motivated by the challenges presented during pandemics such as COVID-19, this article aims to enhance healthcare transparency and expedite treatment processes. The existing centralized medical data management system scatters patient records across disparate hospitals and pharmacies, prompting the necessity for a patient-centric data repository. The integration of blockchain emerges as a viable solution, giving patients control over their information and facilitating seamless sharing with relevant institutions—be it hospitals, pharmacies, or insurance firms. This article outlines a strategic framework for securing medical data based on comprehensive literature review and proposes measures derived from previous studies. Furthermore, the study explores blockchain's application in tracing medicinal supplies, crucial for detecting counterfeit medications within the supply chain. Detailed elucidation of IBM Research's proposed model highlights the potential of blockchain in this domain. Additionally, an extensive comparative analysis of existing models underscores their strengths and limitations in these healthcare applications. Challenges persist in deploying blockchain in developing countries, primarily due to resource limitations, signalling the need for tailored solutions conducive to such environments. This study serves as an exploration, emphasising the need for continued research and innovation in harnessing blockchain's potential for healthcare transformation.

publications.title: A Comparative and Systematic Study of Machine Learning (ML) Approaches for Particulate Matter (PM) Prediction
publications.subtitle: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering, Springer Nature
publications.description: Air quality in metropolitan areas has deteriorated due to growing urbanisation and industrialisation, leading to severe health and significant economic consequences. This paper discusses the particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 forecasting performances of three Machine Learning algorithms: SVM, Random Forest, and k-NN. In our comparisons, we attempt to account for the often overlooked influence of the training dataset on model performance, which significantly influences the accuracy of insights derived from a model. The scope of this study helps determine the numerous international research works to help better analyse the algorithms employed and their execution to generate insights into particulate matter concentrations, which assists in shaping future climate change policies. Our analyses show that SVMs can work with dimensional data, and Random Forests can provide multi-faceted, non-linear regression and classification with higher R2 values than SVM for some datasets. K-NN is frequently applied for preprocessing (data imputation). Furthermore, it has been observed that hybrid models outperform the approaches leveraging independent algorithms.

publications.title: A comprehensive study on skin cancer detection using artificial neural network (ANN) and convolutional neural network (CNN)
publications.subtitle: Clinical eHealth , Elsevier
publications.description: Skin cancer is a significant health risk that requires early detection for effective treatment. This paper discusses two automated techniques, Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), which make use of deep learning techniques for skin cancer detection. Through evaluation of research on skin cancer detection using ANN and CNN, the effectiveness and performance of these techniques in early and efficient diagnosis of skin cancer were established. The study found that ANN and CNN were successful in early detection of skin cancer using different data sets and hybrid models, demonstrating the potential for these technologies to improve accuracy in skin cancer detection. The paper highlights the novelty of using deep learning techniques for skin cancer detection and emphasises the critical need for an automated system for skin lesion recognition to reduce effort and time in the diagnosis process. The possible applications of this study include the development of more efficient and accurate skin cancer detection systems that can lead to earlier diagnosis and improved treatment outcomes. Overall, this research underscores the importance of using advanced technologies, such as ANN and CNN, in the fight against skin cancer and highlights the potential impact of these techniques in improving patient outcomes.

We just won the Most Creative Project at the Cursor x a16z speedrun Hackathon yesterday. 🎉 What we built: Specter. Say you want to edit YouTube videos but have no idea how to use DaVinci Resolve. Normally you're stuck googling tutorials or asking ChatGPT, then trying to translate that into actual clicks on your actual screen. Specter skips that gap. It's an AI agent that lives on your computer, watches your screen, and talks you through whatever app you're in, in real time. Ask it how to do something and it guides you right there in the software, step by step, instead of sending you off to figure it out yourself. It also remembers. Specter keeps a local memory of what you've learned and where you left off, so it's not starting from scratch every time you open the app. The bigger goal: make any application learnable this way, so people outside the engineering world can pick up real tools fast instead of bouncing between tabs trying to piece it together. The biggest question in audit AI right now is the wrong one. "Will this cut hours on our control testing?" And while the answer is yes, it's a question shaped by the first generation of AI tools. This was chat and basic workflow automation, where you paste in a control description, upload data, and the AI tells you what happened. The better question is how much of your company you actually see, and whether you see it in time to fix what's broken. That's the new generation of AI-enabled assurance, where agents sit across hundreds of enterprise applications year round, build persistent memory of how a company's control environment operates, and continuously test the whole population instead of a 1% sample. Issues surface and get remediated in the month they happen, before they compound into a material weakness, a disclosure, and an external audit fee that goes up the next year. That's the real cost of an audit. Hours are the small part. Every audit leader we work with describes some version of this when you ask what their team would do if they weren't buried in manual work all year. Audit becomes the control plane of the enterprise, and we're building Arden (YC P26) to be the infrastructure that powers it.

I'm 17, and I moved to San Francisco alone to fix the thing that killed my best friend. Two years ago, he died in a building collapse in India. Rescue took three days to search the rubble. Drones were on site, but every drone needed its own pilot, and nobody had one picture of what had already been searched. He was alive under there for part of it. So I've spent the last month building software where one person runs an entire robot fleet. When a machine dies mid-job, the nearest one picks up its unfinished work. Everything is logged and replayable, so when someone asks what actually happened, you can prove it instead of guessing. And it turns out this was never just a drone problem. Mining machines, forklifts, farm robots, every fleet hits the same wall the moment one machine drops. If you build or operate robot fleets, I'd genuinely love to hear how you handle a machine dying mid-job. My DMs are open.

I thought finding a cofounder was mostly about chemistry. One week in San Francisco changed my mind. It’s been a wild first week. I watched a SpaceX launch, met some incredibly sharp people, and had conversations that completely shifted how I think about building. But the biggest thing I’ve been thinking about is this: Finding a cofounder is a lot like getting into a relationship. Chemistry matters, but chemistry alone is not enough. Complementary skills are not enough either. You can get along incredibly well with someone, and still be completely wrong for each other as cofounders. What matters first is whether you want to build toward the same future. Do you share the same level of ambition? Do you agree on what is worth spending the next 10 years chasing? Do you actually want to build the same kind of company? Then comes the second part: What is your edge? What is theirs? And when you put the two together, do those edges compound toward the same vision? That’s when the relationship starts to make sense. The other thing that has surprised me about SF is how willing people are to help. You can meet someone who has already built something huge, tell them you’re still at the beginning, and they’ll still give you their time. They’ll challenge your thinking, share what they learned, make an introduction, or point you in a better direction. There’s a ridiculous amount of ambition here, but also a ridiculous amount of generosity. One week down. Still learning, still testing ideas, still figuring out what is worth dedicating the next decade to. But I know why I came here. To build. For the founders here: What made you realize you’d found the right cofounder?

This is my official goodbye to being the internet's list girl. It's been a crazy journey spending the last two years convincing anyone who would give me two seconds of their day to listen to a pitch about making lists. Deciding to step away from building a product I personally loved so much wasn't easy but undoubtedly was the right thing to do. As you might have seen, both Conner and I are no longer actively working on Ditto . Unfortunately, after countless experiments and iterations, we came to the understanding that the ceiling this specific product was not large enough to allow us to reach the sheer impact and scale that we hope to achieve in building this company. But don't worry, the app itself is still being maintained, it's still available to download if someone resonates with the concept. Also because thousands of people would literally crash out if we removed the app. I will always be grateful for our fiercely loyal users. So what have we been doing the last few months then? Conner, myself and our incredible team (both new and old!) have been relentlessly working on a brand new app around the thesis of unlocking the stories from your camera roll. The camera roll is an untapped dataset representing the most accurate, high‑resolution archive of your life — every phase, friendship, and micro‑era in one place, captured and framed exactly how you saw that moment. Our vision was always much bigger than a form factor. My personal motivation stems from an unwavering belief that it's our job to make the internet a more participatory place. How can it be that our only options to engage with the social products is to lurk and doomscroll, become a full-blown content creator or quit it all together. It's clear that the gap for a new social space could not be wider, more obvious, and more important to get right. I'm super excited to introduce you to our new company Beam Camera Roll but for now, felt like I owed my list girl persona a proper goodbye. I'm also very grateful to have the support of our core team, investors and advisors onboard this new journey with us. So much to come. See ya very soon.

publications.title: Elementary Particles
publications.subtitle: International Organisation of Scientific Research's Journal of Applied Physics
publications.description: Elementary-particle Physics deals with the fundamental constituents of matter and their interactions. In the past several decades an enormous amount of experimental information has been accumulated, and many patterns and systematic features have been observed. Highly successful mathematical theories of the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions have been devised and tested. These theories, which are collectively known as the standard model, are almost certainly the correct description of Nature, to first approximation, down to a distance scale 1/1000th the size of the atomic nucleus. There are also speculative but encouraging developments in the attempt to unify these interactions into a simple underlying framework, and even to incorporate quantum gravity in a parameter-free “theory of everything.” In this article we shall attempt to highlight the ways in which information has been organized, and to sketch the outlines of the standard model and its possible extensions. Through this paper, we plan to look at Elementary Particles in detail and address the following questions:● What are elementary particles?● How did we come to know of their existence?● Discoveries behind the elementary particles in bubble chambers.● Standard Model.

I'm happy to share that Aditya Das , Zhiyu Wen , and I won 1st place in the Social Impact track at JacHacks SF! We built SafeRelay, an app that gets an emergency message out when there is no signal. When a natural disaster takes out cell towers, the people who need help most are the ones who suddenly cannot reach anyone, and responders end up working off incomplete reports. Mobile phones with satellite connectivity solve that for the few people carrying one, but not for a neighborhood full of ordinary phones. SafeRelay turns those phones into a peer-to-peer network. You write a distress packet in the field app and it hops phone to phone over Bluetooth, with every device storing it and passing it along. The first phone that gets any connectivity uploads the whole chain to the cloud, where an operations console shows what came in next to live USGS and NWS hazard feeds. Additionally, the Jachammer-powerd web console receives any packets sent by the mobile app, so that first-responders can easily view and prioritize off-grid emergencies. At this hackathon we wrote both the field app and the operations console in Jac, so the packet format, the relay rules and the server all lived in one language instead of three separate stacks. Capacitor handled the mobile shell and CoreBluetooth handled the iOS radio bridge, which is the part you can only really test on physical phones. Special thanks to Jason Mars, Vatsal Shah , Lingjia Tang and the rest of the JacHacks team for running it, and Jaseci Labs for Jac itself. projects.description: Motivated by the work at @CultureLink.ca and inspired by Apple's Assistive Access, we set out on a mission to enhance the accessibility of Android devices for seniors. Rather than expecting seniors to adapt to technology, we recognized the importance of making technology adapt to them. Thus, we developed Android Assist with the aim of simplifying smartphone usage for senior citizens, ensuring they can effortlessly navigate and utilize their devices. projects.title: Signify
projects.description: The current communication gap between deaf and hearing individuals due to the lack of access to sign language interpretation services creates exclusion and isolation of the deaf community. This issue results in a lack of access to essential services, information and opportunities, as well as social and economic disadvantages for the deaf community.Our app aims to address this issue by providing a real-time solution that detects sign language gestures, translates them into written text, and facilitates communication between deaf and hearing individuals, breaking down communication barriers and creating a more inclusive world.Impact:Improved communication: The app enables deaf individuals to communicate more effectively with those who can hear, breaking down communication barriers and allowing for more seamless communication.Increased access to information: The app allows deaf individuals to access information that was previously unavailable to them due to the language barrier. This includes accessing educational materials, job opportunities, and social and cultural events.Enhanced social inclusion: The app promotes social inclusion by allowing deaf individuals to fully participate in society and interact with their hearing peers.

projects.title: Health Canada App
projects.description: By assessing our own needs and thinking about needs of the greater Canadian population, we have created the start of a vision of a more advanced and inclusive healthcare system. I just got back from the 2024 DECA International Career Development Conference. It's still a little surreal to think about. After three years of participating in the Hospitality and Tourism Professional Selling event internationally, this year I took a leap into the unknown and decided to try out the Marketing Communications Series event instead, competing against some of the most talented high schoolers in the world. My risk paid off - I won first place out of more than 1200 competitors! That's not even the best part. In past years, my chapter has never earned more than two top-three placements in any given year, and we have also never won first place in any event. This year, we took away a grand total of SEVEN placements with FIVE first-place trophies. In all honesty, it looks like we set the chapter record! It's absolutely INCREDIBLE - we were all blown away. I'm so proud of everyone. It's all a bit bittersweet, though. ICDC 2024 was my last-ever high school DECA conference, and it's only just fully hit me that transitioning to college means I'll never again get to step into a competition hall ready to start roleplay prep or wait anxiously at the edge of my seat to find out if I'll get called up on stage as a top ten performer. DECA is one of my absolute favorite things, and my experience with it has been unforgettable. I'll treasure all these memories for a long time yet. In the meantime, on to bigger and better things! Perhaps I'll be a DECA judge next year. Who knows? #DECA #ICDC
